newsitem.title: GERMANY: Police detain 110 as German nuclear convoy begins.
newsitem.headline: Police detain 110 as German nuclear convoy begins.

text.p: German police detained more than 100 anti-nuclear activists across the country as controversial shipments of nuclear waste began the first leg of their journey to a storage depot east of Hanover.

Most of the arrests came as a convoy of trucks carried three containers of waste under heavy police guard from the Neckarwestheim power station in southwestern Germany to a nearby railway loading station.

Around 2,000 police guarded the route and demonstrators were banned from going within 50 metres (yards). Police said they had temporarily detained more than 50 people at a protest camp close to the power station as well as other activists in the area.

The slow-moving convoy arrived at the loading station at Walheim after taking three hours to complete the five-km (three-mile) long journey. Shipments from France and Bavaria were due to arrive at Walheim later in the day.

The Lower Saxony state government has said around 30,000 police and border guards will be needed to protect the convoy to the storage depot at Gorleben, making it the biggest security operation in German peacetime history.

Police reported a quieter send-off for a shipment from Grundremmingen in Bavaria. A train containing one container of waste and several wagons of police guards from the plant left without major incident.
The containers will then be coupled together along with a shipment from France to form a rail convoy for the journey to Gorleben.
Officials have said the convoy will stay in Walheim over the weekend and then travel to Gorleben on Monday.
Six activists briefly held up the trucks in Neckarwestheim by forming a human chain across the street. Around 50 fellow protesters outside the police barricade shouted: "Keep it up!"
Police estimated there were around 400 demonstrators along the route, which was guarded by dozens of police vehicles, helicopters, two water cannons and a tank.
The French shipment, from the La Hague reproccessing plant, also crossed the border into Germany on Friday morning.
A spokesman for police in charge of the operation said they were reasonably happy with how things had gone, noting no one had been injured so far.

Protests have heated up ahead of the shipment and suspected anti-nuclear activists have sabotaged rail lines, smashed windows of public buildings in Hamburg and daubed walls with anti-nuclear slogans.
Last year more than 19,000 police and border guards mounted a massive security operation to get a shipment to the plant and police and politicians fear a repeat of mass demonstrations.
Interior Minister Manfred Kanther told parliament on Thursday he would not shrink from a test of strength if it was forced on him by the activists.
